findings.body: Removing the `ALLOWED_HOSTS` check lets `deliver()` POST to any caller-supplied URL. Values such as `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/` or `http://127.0.0.1:1/` are now accepted, and `urllib.request.urlopen` follows redirects, so a public host can bounce the request onto an internal IP. If customer endpoints are required, restrict the scheme to HTTPS, resolve and reject private/link-local/loopback/metadata ranges, and re-validate redirect targets (or restore an explicit allowlist).

summary:
Removing the webhook host allowlist makes `deliver()` an open SSRF sink: any caller-supplied URL is POSTed with `urllib.request.urlopen`, which follows redirects.

That matches the stated goal of customer-owned endpoints, but there is no replacement control — no HTTPS-only scheme check, no block of loopback/link-local/RFC1918/metadata addresses, and no re-validation of redirect targets. A customer- or attacker-controlled `url` can hit `http://169.254.169.254/`, `http://127.0.0.1/`, or an internal service, or bounce there via a 302.

Restore an explicit allowlist, or add equivalent SSRF guards, before merge.

**Recommendation:** request-changes

verification.reason: The patch removes the ALLOWED_HOSTS allowlist that previously rejected non-approved hosts, so deliver() now POSTs via urllib.request.urlopen to any caller-supplied URL, enabling SSRF including metadata/loopback targets and redirect-based internal reach. Critical severity is appropriate for unrestric
